general.temas: The budget law, pensions and proposals to regularize unauthorized construction recur across the front pages. Several newspapers also cover the conviction for Bergamini’s murder, Mattarella’s speech about young people and investigations involving Deutsche Bank and Revolut. Only Corriere della Sera highlights the Toti case and the alleged manipulation of pandemic data in Liguria.
general.motivo_crispacion: Disputes over pensions, taxes and the regularization of unauthorized construction reflect tensions between parties in the governing majority, while disagreements over windfall profits pit opposition parties against one another. In Liguria, Toti’s meetings with a businessman and the alleged manipulation of pandemic data are fueling controversy. Some headlines use accusatory language about antisemitism and Palestine, and the war in Ukraine adds international tension. These are partly offset by informative reports on pensions and the economy and Mattarella’s message about young people.

Corriere della Sera.resumen:
- The front page questions whether changes to the highway code will reduce road deaths.
- Several reports address relations between Toti, Spinelli and other Ligurian officials, including meetings on a yacht and the alleged manipulation of pandemic data.
- The mayor of Genoa rejects the accusations and calls for clarity.
- The governing majority is at odds over the Superbonus and the tax on drinks; in Ukraine, Russian troops are advancing toward Kharkiv.
- Also prominent are reports about Fedez and Camila Giorgi, alongside investment and savings advice.
Corriere della Sera.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “the scandal erupts” and the emphasis on private meetings add drama, although there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
Corriere della Sera.sesgo: The selection devotes considerable space to political controversies in Liguria and disagreements within the governing majority. The headline on the highway code takes a critical stance by asserting that the changes will not reduce road deaths.

la Repubblica.resumen:
- Meloni is pushing for a ban on social media for children under 13 and restrictions up to age 16.
- The investigation into De Gennaro for alleged obstruction is dividing the anti-mafia community; the judge has rejected a request for his arrest.
- Meloni blocks proposals from her own party for an amnesty for unauthorized construction, while Salvini calls for earlier retirement funded by banks.
- The 16-year sentence for Bergamini’s former girlfriend is upheld; a forensic doctor raises doubts about Epstein’s suicide.
- The front page carries reports on Ferragni, Camila Giorgi, a teenager’s funeral, the cancellation of a Russian festival and a speech by Mattarella.
la Repubblica.motivo_populismo: An informative tone predominates, although emotive expressions such as “after the fall” and confrontational wording such as “Salvini challenges his allies” appear, without a clear appeal to the people against the elites.
la Repubblica.sesgo: The front page prioritizes Italian politics, conflicts among its leaders and legal matters. It also combines institutional news with crime stories and emotional personal accounts.

La Stampa.resumen:
- The courts uphold the conviction of the jeweler who killed two robbers and that of Denis Bergamini’s former girlfriend for his murder.
- An investigation into Deutsche Bank uncovers millions of documents; another report presents a forensic analysis of Epstein’s death.
- Investigators are looking into 42 million missing from Revolut and transactions by 22 suspicious clients.
- The front page addresses the possible regularization of unauthorized construction, pensions and tensions between opposition parties over the budget.
- Ukraine and Russia attack bridges; the pope rules out an early resignation for now.
La Stampa.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “earthquake,” “major investigation” and “42 million missing” add drama, although informative headlines predominate, without explicitly pitting the people against the elites.
La Stampa.sesgo: The selection prioritizes court cases, financial investigations and conflicts, with some reports taking an exposé-style approach. The presentation of Epstein’s death emphasizes the murder theory and its alleged cover-up.

Il Giornale.resumen:
- Conte and Schlein vote against an antisemitism bill they had championed.
- The EU forecasts an Italian deficit of 2.9% in 2026 and is considering a possible exit from the infringement procedure.
- Budget negotiations address changes to pensions and health care; the League is pushing for retirement under the quota 64 scheme.
- Isabella Internò’s 16-year sentence for the murder of footballer Bergamini is upheld.
- Other reports include investigations into Deutsche Bank and Revolut, statements by Leo XIV and Mattarella, and accusations against Hannoun.
Il Giornale.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “U-turn” and “useful idiot of Islam” introduce disparagement and confrontation, although many headlines maintain an informative tone.
Il Giornale.sesgo: A critical approach toward figures on the left is apparent, especially in headlines about Conte, Schlein and Hannoun. The selection also highlights statements favorable to Meloni and proposals from the League.

Il Fatto Quotidiano.resumen:
- The relationship between building amnesties and elections is examined, from Craxi and Berlusconi to Meloni.
- Around 2,800 possible cases of improper reimbursement for diabetes drugs used for weight loss have been identified in Lombardy.
- Nordio calls for consideration of a proposal to include protections for crime victims in the Constitution; a spokesperson raises concerns about the caregivers law.
- Kaja Kallas questions her exclusion from the European negotiating group on the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
- The front page includes health, sports, culture and television stories, among them the death of Mitzi Amoroso and a review of U2’s new album.
Il Fatto Quotidiano.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “cheats,” “rebels” and “their worst fear comes true” lend an accusatory and emotional tone, although explicit confrontation between the people and the elites does not predominate.
Il Fatto Quotidiano.sesgo: The front page takes a critical approach to building amnesties and highlights inequalities in access to medicines. It also gives space to personal accounts and highly emotive headlines.

opiniones.comunista:
I see a class contradiction on the front pages: while Italy’s possible exit from the deficit procedure is celebrated, the OECD reports that real income per person has fallen by 1%. Public finances cannot be judged by their balance alone, but by the lives they make possible for working people.

The proposal to fund early retirement with resources from the banks opens up a necessary debate, even if it has not yet been approved. I would go further: banking should serve social needs under public and democratic control, not decide our future according to private profitability.

I also support a public health care system capable of guaranteeing necessary treatments regardless of each patient’s ability to pay. The cases of improper reimbursements in Lombardy require oversight, but also a medicines policy that puts health before profit. Collective ownership is part of that answer.
opiniones.anarquista:
The proposal to ban social media for children under 13 presents control as protection. I do not deny the risks, but I doubt that a ban imposed from above will teach people how to face them. I prefer digital education, guidance and spaces where young people, families and teachers decide together, without handing all authority to the state or the platforms.

I am also concerned that, after decades of waiting, the caregivers law could be rushed through. Caregiving should not be a solitary burden or be left at the mercy of negotiations between parties. I support mutual aid networks and services organized with the direct participation of those who provide and receive care. Self-management does not mean abandoning anyone: it means sharing resources and decisions. For me, individual freedom is real only when we can sustain it collectively.
opiniones.liberal:
The proposal to ban social media for children under thirteen strikes me as an overly convenient response: it shifts to the state decisions that belong first and foremost to families. Protecting children matters, but a blanket ban deserves rigorous scrutiny of its effectiveness and its costs to freedom.

I am also wary of funding new early-retirement promises by passing the bill to the banks. Taxes do not disappear simply because a politically convenient payer is chosen: they can affect credit, savings and investment. I prefer low taxes, responsible public finances and a pension system that does not jeopardize the future of young people.

A limited state is not an indifferent state: it must protect rights, enforce the rules and leave room for people to decide how to live, with information and responsibility.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I want an Italy that decides for itself, protects its borders and demands compliance with its laws. The mayor of Lampedusa joining Brothers of Italy should serve to bring one demand to the fore: strict immigration control, not a policy dictated from Brussels or by those who confuse sovereignty with intolerance.

I also support limiting minors’ access to social media. The family must regain authority in the face of platforms that have turned our children’s attention into a business. But protecting traditions requires more than speeches: it requires strong schools and respect for those who educate.

And I am wary of pension promises without clear funding. Debt does not disappear because parties fight over how to distribute it: it ends up falling on families and future generations. National responsibility starts with telling them the truth.
opiniones.centro:
I see the Italian debate on pensions as a test of political responsibility. The proposal to bring forward retirement deserves examination, but announcing that it will be funded with resources from the banks is no substitute for a convincing explanation of its costs and sustainability. Protecting those who have worked all their lives also requires us not to pass uncertain commitments on to young people.

On the regularization of unauthorized construction, I would argue for a clear distinction: resolving minor irregularities must not become a signal of leniency toward abuses. Rules need to be fair, understandable and applied consistently. I would rather see the government and opposition negotiate concrete reforms, with transparent costs, than compete with promises that will be difficult to keep. A dynamic market and strong social protection need the same foundation: reliable institutions and credible public finances.
